corrected_value.authors: Medvec, V. H., Madey, S. F., & Gilovich, T.
corrected_value.title: When less is more: Counterfactual thinking and satisfaction among Olympic medalists.

decisions.quote:
This study was a conceptual replication of the first studies in
Medvec et al. (1995) and McGraw et al. (2005) with a few key
differences. Medvec et al. (1995) used silent video footage from
National Broadcasting Company (NBC) of the 1992 Olympic
games to analyze facial expressions of 15 bronze and 20 silver
medalists.

decisions.quote:
In
sum, this research demonstrated consistent findings with both
Medvec et al. (1995) and McGraw et al. (2005) finding support for
both ex post and ex ante counterfactual thinking among Olympic
athletes.
decisions.reason: After resolving row 782 to Medvec, Madey, and Gilovich (1995) (blind target 0), both shipped and blind correctly code the replication outcome as 'successful'. The authors explicitly state in the General Discussion that they conceptually replicated Medvec et al. (1995), confirming that bronze medalists were significantly more likely to display smiles than silver medalists both in the full sample and when restricted to silver and bronze medalists.

decisions.quote:
Using automated facial expression analysis, we conceptually
replicated Medvec et al. (1995). We confirmed the phenomenon
that bronze medalists appeared happier than silver medalists after
competition in Olympic events. Our results are consistent with the
theory that facial expressions of Olympic medalists were influenced by two prominent types of counterfactual thinking:
category-based and expectation-based counterfactuals.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind correctly classify the record as a 'replication'. The authors collected a new sample of 413 Olympic medal-stand photographs from the 2000-2016 Summer Olympic Games and encoded facial expressions using automated FACS software to re-test the published counterfactual thinking findings of Medvec et al. (1995).

decisions.quote:
If medalists were using expectations formed prior to an Olympic
event (McGraw et al., 2005), we would expect that medal expectations would be correlated with the presence of smiles and they
were, Wald "2(2) ! 4.316, p ! .014. Individuals performing better
than expectations were more likely to exhibit a smile (MBetter !
2.660, SE ! 0.205) than people performing worse than expected
(MWorse ! 0.899, SE ! 0.386), t(389) ! 3.863, p # .001. These
results suggests that both ex post and ex ante counterfactuals
influenced medalists’ emotions.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication (b7f518d6f27c1b3209c4093ab5badc3771df5c04207bb4e66f6312dadcc3efb8.json) linked the sole shipped row (input_row_index 782: Medvec, Madey, & Gilovich, 1995, 10.1037/0022-3514.69.4.603) to blind target_index 0; the prior state file does not exist. The primary text explicitly frames its study as 'a conceptual replication of the first studies in Medvec et al. (1995) and McGraw et al. (2005)' (lines 204-205) using automated facial expression encoding of 413 Olympic medal stand photographs and Sports Illustrated medal predictions. In the Results section (lines 378-385), the authors empirically re-test McGraw et al.'s (2005) expectation-based (ex ante) counterfactual finding—that athletes performing better than prior expectations display more positive emotion (smiles) than those performing worse than expected—reporting a significant effect of medal expectations on smiles (Wald chi-square(2) = 4.316, p = .014; M_Better = 2.660 vs. M_Worse = 0.899, t(389) = 3.863, p < .001), and concluding in the General Discussion (lines 1192-1196) that their findings were consistent with both Medvec et al. (1995) and McGraw et al. (2005). Reference identity is verified in the reference list (lines 1284-1285) and Crossref metadata (10.1016/j.jesp.2004.09.001). Because McGraw, Mellers, & Tetlock (2005) is an independent study by different authors testing ex ante expectations in the 2000 Summer Olympics rather than an alternate report of Medvec, Madey, & Gilovich (1995, 1992 Summer Olympics ex post category comparisons), it is genuinely absent from all shipped rows.
